stages.name: requirement
stages.what: A row in requirements/software_requirements.csv: ID, title, shall-statement, verification method, acceptance criteria.
stages.why: The requirement is the contract. Tests exist to prove it, not the other way around.
stages.failures: A vague 'shall respond quickly' is untestable — 250 ms is.

stages.name: test
stages.what: A pytest function marked @pytest.mark.requirement("REQ-...") asserting the acceptance criteria.
stages.why: The marker makes the requirement→test link machine-readable, not tribal knowledge.
stages.failures: --strict-markers rejects unregistered markers; a typo'd requirement ID silently breaks the chain.

stages.name: execution
stages.what: pytest runs the test against a live DUT child process launched by the session fixture.
stages.why: Results only mean something against a running system with controlled startup and cleanup.
stages.failures: A leaked DUT from an earlier run can make this run's results meaningless.

stages.name: result
stages.what: Pass/fail per testcase, written as JUnit XML to evidence/junit/test-results.xml.
stages.why: JUnit is the machine-readable result format CI systems and audits consume.
stages.failures: No junitxml flag = no machine-readable result, only console text.

stages.name: evidence
stages.what: JUnit XML plus the DUT log (evidence/logs/dut.log), cross-referenced from requirements/traceability.csv.
stages.why: The traceability row is the auditable sentence: 'REQ-X is verified by test T, evidence at path E.'
stages.failures: Evidence is gitignored and regenerated — if you need it for an audit, collect it before the next run overwrites it.
